thread: To keep something is to lose it: the preserved likeness replaces the living thing
summary: Each piece asks what we do to a thing when we hold on to it. Ruskin argues that restoring an old building does not preserve it, because the scraped and replaced surface is a copy that pretends to be the original, and that the honest course is to care for it and then let it go. Keats images a vase on which a chase and a kiss are fixed for ever, and finds the permanence both sweeter and colder than the life it pictures. Poe dramatises a painter so absorbed in capturing his wife on canvas that the portrait gains life exactly as she loses it. Mitchell sings around it: she recalls clouds, love and life, and admits that what she remembers is the picture she made of them, not the thing itself.

pieces.essay: Ruskin argues it: the building that is restored is no longer the building, and the loving hand that rebuilds it has told a lie about the past.
pieces.poem: Keats images it: the lovers on the urn never age and never kiss, and the speaker cannot decide whether that is a blessing.
pieces.story: Poe dramatises it: the painter's devotion to the likeness drains the sitter, and he realises what he has done only when the work is finished.
pieces.song: Mitchell sings around it: each verse looks again at something loved and finds that her memory had been holding an illusion in its place.

forYou: A pontianak story, and any story built on a haunting, lives on this problem: the version of the dead woman that survives in memory or legend is not the woman, and your drafts can ask who paid for it.
